questions.subject: dm
questions.title: Shifted geometric divisibility 1
questions.prompt: Prove 3 divides (4)^n-1 for n>=0 by induction.

solution.text: Let P(n) assert that 3 divides 4^n-1 for all integers n>=0. Basis: 4^0-1=0=3*0.
Inductive hypothesis: let k>=0 be arbitrary and assume 4^k-1=3*m for some integer m.
Substitute the hypothesis: 4^(k+1)-1=3*(4*m+1). Let t=4*m+1. It is an integer, so P(k+1) holds.
By the principle of mathematical induction, 3 divides 4^n-1 for every integer n>=0.

questions.conceptNote: Establish the correct basis, state a hypothesis for arbitrary earlier indices, and justify every transition to the next case.

rubric.criterion: Statement/domain and computed basis
Explicit inductive hypothesis
Algebra exposing the hypothesis
Successor justification (named integer factor for divisibility)
Conclusion citing the appropriate induction principle

questions.subject: dm
questions.title: A congruence partition
questions.prompt: On A={1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9}, x R y iff x=y (mod 3). Prove equivalence and list the partition.

solution.text: Reflexivity follows from x-x=0. Symmetry follows by negating a divisible difference. Transitivity follows by adding two divisible differences.
The classes are the equal-remainder groups: {1,4,7}; {2,5,8}; {3,6,9}.
They are disjoint and cover A, so this is the partition.

questions.conceptNote: Equivalence means reflexive, symmetric and transitive; partial order replaces symmetry with antisymmetry. Classes are relative to the specified universe.

solution.text: Step 1: add edge AB (weight 2). Consider edges in nondecreasing weight order. It is a minimum-weight edge joining two current components, so no cycle is formed.
Step 2: add edge BC (weight 2). It is a minimum-weight edge joining two current components, so no cycle is formed.
Step 3: add edge EF (weight 2). It is a minimum-weight edge joining two current components, so no cycle is formed.

questions.subject: dm
questions.title: Euler and Hamilton reasoning
questions.prompt: For the star K1,4, determine whether an Euler path and a Hamilton path exist. Explain.

solution.text: The centre has degree 4; the 4 leaves each have degree 1.
The graph has 4 odd-degree vertices, which is more than 2. Hence there is no Euler path.
Every leaf would be an endpoint of a Hamilton path, but there are more than two leaves. Hence there is no Hamilton path.

solution.text: If f(x)=f(y), then 3*x+1=3*y+1, so x=y. Thus f is injective.
All outputs are congruent to 1 modulo 3. The integer 2 is not in that residue class and has no preimage.
Hence f is not surjective onto Z.

questions.subject: dm
questions.title: Slot 1 Q1b: divisibility variant 6
questions.prompt: Write a FULL typed proof by mathematical induction that 15 divides 4^(2*n)-1 for all integers n>=0. State P(n), compute the basis, state the hypothesis with an integer m, derive P(k+1), name its integer factor, and conclude. Checkpoints alone are not the answer.

solution.text: Let P(n) be the statement that 15 divides 4^(2*n)-1, for every integer n>=0. Basis: at n=0, 4^(2*0)-1=0=15*0. Thus P(0) holds.
Inductive hypothesis: let k>=0 be arbitrary and assume P(k). Then 4^(2*k)-1=15*m for some integer m.

For the inductive step, start from the expression in P(k+1):
4^(2*(k+1))-1
= 16*(4^(2*k)-1)+15. This exposes the expression in the inductive hypothesis.

Substituting the hypothesis gives
4^(2*(k+1))-1=15*(16*m+1).
Let t=16*m+1. Since k and m are integers and all powers here have nonnegative integer exponents, t is an integer. Hence 15 divides the expression in P(k+1).
The basis and inductive step have been proved. By the principle of mathematical induction, 15 divides 4^(2*n)-1 for every integer n>=0.

rubric.criterion: Statement, domain and computed divisible basis
Explicit inductive hypothesis with integer m
Algebra starting at P(k+1) and exposing P(k)
Substitution and named integer factor
Quantified conclusion citing mathematical induction

questions.title: Slot 1 Q3: two-colour triangle under rotations
questions.prompt: Colour each of the 3 labelled vertices using X/Y. All 8 colourings are allowed. Two are equivalent iff related by a rotation only. Prove this is an equivalence relation, list the complete partition and count the classes.

solution.text: The identity rotation proves reflexivity. Every allowed symmetry has an allowed inverse, proving symmetry. Composition of allowed symmetries is allowed, proving transitivity.

A class is the orbit obtained by applying every allowed symmetry to one colouring. Positions are labelled in clockwise order. R=Red, G=Green, B=Blue (or the two stated colours); repeated identical words are listed only once.

The complete universe is A={XXX,XXY,XYX,XYY,YXX,YXY,YYX,YYY}. The distinct classes are:
{XXX}; {XXY,XYX,YXX}; {XYY,YXY,YYX}; {YYY}.
There are 4 classes. Their sizes sum to 8; the classes are disjoint and cover A.

questions.subject: dm
questions.title: Slot 1 Q4: non-homogeneous variant 5
questions.prompt: Solve a_n=5*a_(n-1)-8*a_(n-2)+4*a_(n-3)+n^3, n>=3; a_0=1,a_1=0,a_2=2. Find the characteristic equation and roots, particular solution coefficients, and closed form with all constants.

solution.text: The associated homogeneous characteristic equation is r^3-5*r^2+8*r-4=(r-1)*(r-2)^2=0. Thus its roots, with multiplicity, are 1,2,2.
The homogeneous solution is C1*(1)+C2*(2^n)+C3*(n*2^n). Repeated roots require successive powers of n.
The forcing is n^3, with base 1. This base has multiplicity 1 in the characteristic polynomial. Try p_n=A*(n^4)+B*(n^3)+C*(n^2)+D*(n). The factor n^1 avoids overlap with the homogeneous solution.

Substitute p_n into p_n-(5)*p_(n-1)-(-8)*p_(n-2)-(4)*p_(n-3)=n^3. After expansion and cancellation of 1^n, equate coefficients of n^3 down to n^0:
4*A=1
-54*A+3*B=0
196*A-27*B+2*C=0
-201*A+49*B-9*C+1*D=0
Therefore A=(1/4),B=(9/2),C=(145/4),D=156, and p_n=(1/4)*(n^4)+(9/2)*(n^3)+(145/4)*(n^2)+156*(n).

Add homogeneous and particular parts. The initial conditions give:
1*C1+1*C2+0*C3=1-(0)
1*C1+2*C2+2*C3=0-(197)
1*C1+4*C2+8*C3=2-(497)
Solving yields C1=297,C2=-296,C3=49.

Hence a_n=297-296*(2^n)+49*(n*2^n)+(1/4)*(n^4)+(9/2)*(n^3)+(145/4)*(n^2)+156*(n), for every integer n>=0. Substituting the first 3 terms gives a_0=1,a_1=0,a_2=2; substitution into the recurrence gives the stated forcing. This, with the initial values, determines the sequence uniquely.

questions.subject: dm
questions.title: Slot 1 Q5: Kruskal variant 5
questions.prompt: Constructed graph (the reported sketch's exact edges were not supplied): V={A,B,C,D,E,F,G}, edges AB(3),BC(1),AC(2),CD(2),BD(4),DE(6),CE(5),EF(7),DF(5),FG(8),EG(9). Use Kruskal. Type each accepted AND rejected candidate in order with a reason, stop at six accepted edges, and state total weight. Any valid tie order is allowed. (Sort 2, six additions 6, spanning/total 2 marks.)

solution.text: Sort all edges by nondecreasing weight (break ties by the displayed edge order): BC(1),AC(2),CD(2),AB(3),BD(4),CE(5),DF(5),DE(6),EF(7),FG(8),EG(9). Start with seven singleton components. (2 marks.)
Step 1: add edge BC (weight 1). It joins different components and is a lightest eligible edge. Components now: {A}; {B,C}; {D}; {E}; {F}; {G}. (1 mark.)
Step 2: add edge AC (weight 2). It joins different components and is a lightest eligible edge. Components now: {A,B,C}; {D}; {E}; {F}; {G}. (1 mark.)
Step 3: add edge CD (weight 2). It joins different components and is a lightest eligible edge. Components now: {A,B,C,D}; {E}; {F}; {G}. (1 mark.)
Reject edge AB (weight 3): its endpoints already lie in the same component, so it creates a cycle.
Reject edge BD (weight 4): its endpoints already lie in the same component, so it creates a cycle.
Step 4: add edge CE (weight 5). It joins different components and is a lightest eligible edge. Components now: {A,B,C,D,E}; {F}; {G}. (1 mark.)
Step 5: add edge DF (weight 5). It joins different components and is a lightest eligible edge. Components now: {A,B,C,D,E,F}; {G}. (1 mark.)
Reject edge DE (weight 6): its endpoints already lie in the same component, so it creates a cycle.
Reject edge EF (weight 7): its endpoints already lie in the same component, so it creates a cycle.
Step 6: add edge FG (weight 8). It joins different components and is a lightest eligible edge. Components now: {A,B,C,D,E,F,G}. (1 mark.)

Finally all seven vertices are connected with six accepted edges. Stop; later edges are not examined. This is an MST by Kruskal's algorithm; total weight = 1 + 2 + 2 + 5 + 5 + 8 = 23. (2 marks for spanning-tree check and sum.)

questions.conceptNote: Sort by weight and check components at every candidate. Ties allow alternatives; cycle edges are rejected and the total is compulsory.

questions.prompt: Construct a complete truth table for ((p -> q) ^ (~q -> r)) -> (p -> (q v r)). Include columns p -> q; ~q -> r; ((p -> q) ^ (~q -> r)) -> (p -> (q v r)). Classify the final column.

solution.text: Write 8 rows, T before F, with p changing slowest. (1 mark for row order; 1 each for the three stages, or 3 for the two compared expressions; 1 for the conclusion.)
Columns: p | q | r | p -> q | ~q -> r | ((p -> q) ^ (~q -> r)) -> (p -> (q v r))
T | T | T | T | T | T
T | T | F | T | T | T
T | F | T | F | T | T
T | F | F | F | F | T
F | T | T | T | T | T
F | T | F | T | T | T
F | F | T | T | T | T
F | F | F | T | F | T
The final column is a tautology because all entries are T.

questions.conceptNote: Work from the innermost implication outward; an implication is false only for T -> F.

questions.subject: dm
questions.title: Slot 1 Q1b: divisibility variant 7
questions.prompt: Write a FULL typed proof by mathematical induction that 13 divides 3^(n+2)+4^(2*n+1) for all integers n>=0. State P(n), compute the basis, state the hypothesis with an integer m, derive P(k+1), name its integer factor, and conclude. Checkpoints alone are not the answer.

solution.text: Let P(n) be the statement that 13 divides 3^(n+2)+4^(2*n+1), for every integer n>=0. Basis: at n=0, 3^(0+2)+4^(2*0+1)=13=13*1. Thus P(0) holds.
Inductive hypothesis: let k>=0 be arbitrary and assume P(k). Then 3^(k+2)+4^(2*k+1)=13*m for some integer m.

For the inductive step, start from the expression in P(k+1):
3^(k+3)+4^(2*k+3)
= 3*(3^(k+2)+4^(2*k+1))+13*4^(2*k+1). This exposes the expression in the inductive hypothesis.

Substituting the hypothesis gives
3^(k+3)+4^(2*k+3)=13*(3*m+4^(2*k+1)).
Let t=3*m+4^(2*k+1). Since k and m are integers and all powers here have nonnegative integer exponents, t is an integer. Hence 13 divides the expression in P(k+1).
The basis and inductive step have been proved. By the principle of mathematical induction, 13 divides 3^(n+2)+4^(2*n+1) for every integer n>=0.

questions.title: Slot 1 Q4: non-homogeneous variant 6
questions.prompt: Solve a_n=6*a_(n-1)-9*a_(n-2)+3^n, n>=2; a_0=2,a_1=9. Find the characteristic equation and roots, particular solution coefficients, and closed form with all constants.

solution.text: The associated homogeneous characteristic equation is r^2-6*r+9=(r-3)^2=0. Thus its roots, with multiplicity, are 3,3.
The homogeneous solution is C1*(3^n)+C2*(n*3^n). Repeated roots require successive powers of n.
The forcing is 3^n, with base 3. This base has multiplicity 2 in the characteristic polynomial. Try p_n=A*(n^2*3^n). The factor n^2 avoids overlap with the homogeneous solution.

Substitute p_n into p_n-(6)*p_(n-1)-(-9)*p_(n-2)=3^n. After expansion and cancellation of 3^n, equate coefficients of n^0 down to n^0:
2*A=1
Therefore A=(1/2), and p_n=(1/2)*(n^2*3^n).

Add homogeneous and particular parts. The initial conditions give:
1*C1+0*C2=2-(0)
3*C1+3*C2=9-((3/2))
Solving yields C1=2,C2=(1/2).

Hence a_n=2*(3^n)+(1/2)*(n*3^n)+(1/2)*(n^2*3^n), for every integer n>=0. Substituting the first 2 terms gives a_0=2,a_1=9; substitution into the recurrence gives the stated forcing. This, with the initial values, determines the sequence uniquely.

questions.subject: dm
questions.title: Slot 1 Q5: Kruskal variant 6
questions.prompt: Constructed graph (the reported sketch's exact edges were not supplied): V={A,B,C,D,E,F,G}, edges AB(1),BC(2),AC(3),CD(2),BD(5),DE(4),CE(6),EF(3),DF(7),FG(9),EG(8). Use Kruskal. Type each accepted AND rejected candidate in order with a reason, stop at six accepted edges, and state total weight. Any valid tie order is allowed. (Sort 2, six additions 6, spanning/total 2 marks.)

solution.text: Sort all edges by nondecreasing weight (break ties by the displayed edge order): AB(1),BC(2),CD(2),AC(3),EF(3),DE(4),BD(5),CE(6),DF(7),EG(8),FG(9). Start with seven singleton components. (2 marks.)
Step 1: add edge AB (weight 1). It joins different components and is a lightest eligible edge. Components now: {A,B}; {C}; {D}; {E}; {F}; {G}. (1 mark.)
Step 2: add edge BC (weight 2). It joins different components and is a lightest eligible edge. Components now: {A,B,C}; {D}; {E}; {F}; {G}. (1 mark.)
Step 3: add edge CD (weight 2). It joins different components and is a lightest eligible edge. Components now: {A,B,C,D}; {E}; {F}; {G}. (1 mark.)
Reject edge AC (weight 3): its endpoints already lie in the same component, so it creates a cycle.
Step 4: add edge EF (weight 3). It joins different components and is a lightest eligible edge. Components now: {A,B,C,D}; {E,F}; {G}. (1 mark.)
Step 5: add edge DE (weight 4). It joins different components and is a lightest eligible edge. Components now: {A,B,C,D,E,F}; {G}. (1 mark.)
Reject edge BD (weight 5): its endpoints already lie in the same component, so it creates a cycle.
Reject edge CE (weight 6): its endpoints already lie in the same component, so it creates a cycle.
Reject edge DF (weight 7): its endpoints already lie in the same component, so it creates a cycle.
Step 6: add edge EG (weight 8). It joins different components and is a lightest eligible edge. Components now: {A,B,C,D,E,F,G}. (1 mark.)

Finally all seven vertices are connected with six accepted edges. Stop; later edges are not examined. This is an MST by Kruskal's algorithm; total weight = 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 8 = 20. (2 marks for spanning-tree check and sum.)
